title: The first sin
hookLine: Augustine taught that Adam's guilt is inherited; the Orthodox speak of inheriting mortality and a wounded nature, not guilt

lines: THE THING YOU DECIDED NOT TO DO.
THE GOOD THAT I WOULD I DO NOT.
cards: Why is it so easy to do the very thing you just decided not to do? The second cookie. The sharp reply.
The phone, picked up again. In Romans, Paul writes: "For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do."

Christian readers have heard more than a bad day in it: a pull in the grain of being human, there before anyone chooses it. Christians name where that pull comes from, and tell its story in more than one way.

teach.b: Original sin doesn't mean an unusual sin. It means the sin at the origin: Adam and Eve in the garden, reaching for the fruit, and everything that followed.
Day three hundred thirteen called sin a condition everyone shares.
Paul ties the story to all of us: "as by one man sin entered into the world, and death by sin; and so death passed upon all men, for that all have sinned."
Christian teaching, East and West, says something went wrong at the start and reached everyone. They differ on what was passed down.
Augustine, the bishop in North Africa, taught that Adam's guilt itself is inherited: in Adam all humanity sinned, and every child is born sharing that guilt as well as its damage.
In the West, Catholics and Protestants build on his reading, with different stresses.
The Orthodox churches of the East tell it differently. What we inherit from Adam, they say, is not his guilt but mortality, and a wounded nature that leans toward sin.
A newborn isn't guilty of anything, but is born into a world where death and the pull toward wrong are already in the air. Guilt, in Orthodox teaching, is for sins a person actually commits.
Here's what both readings refuse to say: that a person is worthless.
Before the garden, Genesis says God looked at everything he had made, "and, behold, it was very good." The fall doesn't undo that. Wounded, in every telling.

how: Christians speak of original sin when they teach about baptism and grace; Western churches build on Augustine's teaching of inherited guilt in different ways, while Orthodox churches teach that people inherit mortality and a wounded nature, not Adam's guilt.

o: the sin at the origin, and what it left in us
the first sin a child commits on their own
a sin nobody has ever thought of before

games.q: the first sin — tap the pairs.

s: original sin means a sin nobody has thought of before
it means the sin at the origin, in the garden, and what it left in everyone.
Orthodox churches teach that a newborn is guilty of Adam's sin
they teach that people inherit mortality and a wounded nature, and guilt is for sins a person commits.
Paul writes about doing the evil he doesn't want to do
"for the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do."

games.q: a baby is born. according to the Orthodox reading of the story of Adam, what has that baby inherited?
o: mortality and a wounded nature, but not guilt.
games.why: Orthodox teachers say we inherit death and a nature that leans toward sin, not Adam's guilt. Augustine, in the West, taught that guilt is inherited too.

practice: Think back over the last day, without hunting for your worst moment, and find one small place where you felt a tug you didn't want to follow: impatience, a little lie, wanting to be first.
Look at it the way a doctor looks at a bruise, honestly and without disgust, and name it quietly. If you pray, hold it out to God and ask for healing; if not, let it be seen, and breathe with it.

wordCard.voice: Original sin. The sin at the origin, and what it left in us. Augustine said guilt; the Orthodox say mortality and a wounded nature.

orig.note: Latin: original sin, the sin at the origin. A Western phrase, associated with Augustine.

carryVoice: Your line: wounded, not worthless. The wound is real, and so is the very good. See you tomorrow.
